topics.deep:
- **Cooperating process** = one that can **affect or be affected by** other processes executing in the system (share data or communicate); independent processes do not. Needs **IPC** (shared memory, message passing) and synchronisation.
- **Race condition:** several processes access and manipulate same data concurrently and outcome depends on the **order/relative timing** of access. Example: two processes doing `count++` and `count--`; each is load, modify, store, so interleaving can give 4, 5 or 6 instead of 5.
- **Critical-section problem:** structure = entry section, critical section, exit section, remainder section. A correct solution must give:
- **Mutual exclusion** - only one process in CS at a time.
- **Progress** - if none in CS, selection of next cannot be postponed indefinitely and only processes not in remainder section take part.
- **Bounded waiting** - bound on the number of times others enter CS after a process has requested entry (prevents starvation).
- (No assumption about CPU speed; "deadlock freedom" or "priority" is not one of the three formal requirements.)
- **Solutions:** software (Peterson for 2 processes; **Bakery algorithm for n processes**), hardware (TestAndSet, Swap/compare-and-swap, disabling interrupts), OS (mutex locks, semaphores), high-level (monitors).
- **Peterson's algorithm:** shared `int turn; boolean flag[2];` Process i: flag[i]=true; turn=j; while(flag[j] && turn==j); CS; flag[i]=false. Satisfies mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting; only for **two** processes; fails on modern out-of-order CPUs without memory barriers.
- **Semaphore** (Dijkstra): integer variable accessed (apart from initialisation) only through two **atomic** operations **wait(P) and signal(V)**. wait: `while(S<=0); S--;` signal: `S++`. **Binary semaphore** (0/1, like mutex lock) vs **counting semaphore** (any non-negative integer, count = available resource instances; initial value = number of instances). A counting semaphore ranges over unrestricted integer domain. Can be implemented in software or hardware. Busy waiting version = **spinlock**; blocking version uses a queue plus block()/wakeup().
- **Mutex vs semaphore:** mutex has ownership (locker unlocks), binary semaphore has none; semaphore can signal between processes.
- **Classical problems:** **Bounded buffer (producer-consumer)** - semaphores mutex=1, empty=n, full=0. **Readers-writers** - many readers may read simultaneously, but a writer needs exclusive access; first (readers' preference) can starve writers, second variant can starve readers. **Dining philosophers** - 5 philosophers, 5 chopsticks; naive solution can deadlock; fix with at most 4 seated or odd/even order. Sleeping barber.
- **Monitor:** high-level abstraction; only one process active inside at a time; condition variables with wait/signal.
- **Windows synchronisation:** in kernel uses **spinlocks/interrupt masking**; outside the kernel provides **dispatcher objects** (mutex, semaphore, event, timer) and critical-section objects. Dispatcher objects can be signaled/non-signaled.
- **Linux synchronisation:** atomic integers, spinlocks, mutex locks, semaphores, reader-writer locks.
- **Buffering:** a buffer is a memory area holding data in transit between two devices or between a device and an application; purposes: speed mismatch, transfer-size mismatch, **copy semantics**. Types: single, double, circular buffering. **Cache** holds a copy of data; **buffer** may hold the only copy. **Spooling** holds output for a device that cannot interleave (printer).
- **Simple batch system:** **resident monitor** controls sequential job transfer (automatic job sequencing); components: card reader, memory with monitor and user program area, **control cards** (JCL).
- **Typical traps:** semaphore is an integer, not a boolean or a process; wait/signal must be atomic; mutual exclusion alone is not a full solution; Peterson works for exactly 2; readers-writers - two readers never conflict.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) final value of shared counter for a given interleaving; (2) initial value for mutex/empty/full semaphores; (3) which classical problem uses a given semaphore pattern; (4) what happens if signal omitted or wait order reversed (deadlock); (5) difference between binary/counting semaphore; (6) spinlock vs blocking; (7) Bakery algorithm purpose; (8) test-and-set lock reasoning; (9) monitor vs semaphore; (10) definition of busy waiting and priority inversion.

topics.title: 6. Deadlocks
topics.theory:
- **Four necessary conditions (Coffman):** **Mutual exclusion** (at least one non-sharable resource), **Hold and wait**, **No preemption** (resource can't be forcibly taken — "preemption" is *not* a condition), **Circular wait**.
- **Handling:** **Prevention** (negate one condition), **Avoidance** (Banker's algorithm — safe state check), **Detection & recovery** (wait-for graph; kill process/preempt resources), **Ignore** (ostrich — Unix/Windows).
- **Safe state** ⇒ no deadlock; unsafe state *may* lead to deadlock. Resource-allocation graph: cycle with single-instance resources ⇒ deadlock.
- **Starvation** (indefinite postponement; fix by aging) differs from deadlock.

Therefore, it is fundamentally associated with the page replacement function within operating systems.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement of solution to critical section problems in an operating system?
qs.sol:
A critical-section solution requires mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting.

Hold and wait is a deadlock condition, not one of those requirements.
qs.rel: Critical-section requirements: mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting. Not requirements: deadlock detection, fairness by priority, minimal CPU time. Know the three exactly.

qs.stem: Which one of these is not a condition for Resource Deadlock?
qs.sol:
For a deadlock to occur, four specific conditions must hold simultaneously:

Mutual Exclusion (Non-shareable resources)

Hold and Wait

No Preemption

Circular Wait

 No Preemption is the actual condition required for deadlock. If "Preemption" is allowed, the operating system can forcibly take a resource away from a process to give it to another, which actually helps prevent or break a deadlock.
qs.rel: Coffman conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Starvation, aging and priority inversion are not conditions. All four must hold together.

qs.stem: In which of the following condition of Deadlock Prevention, at least one resource must be non-sharable?
qs.sol: Mutual exclusion means at least one resource is non-sharable. It is one of the necessary deadlock conditions.
qs.rel: Mutual exclusion cannot be removed for non-sharable resources (printer), hence prevention usually targets hold-and-wait, no-preemption or circular wait (resource ordering).

qs.stem:
Which of the following statement(s) is/are true about CPU scheduling algorithm?
 I. Shortest Remaining Time First scheduling may cause starvation.
 II. Round Robin is better than First Come First Serve in terms of response time.
qs.sol: CONCEPT: Preemptive scheduling can repeatedly favor short jobs, while time-sliced scheduling gives each ready process periodic CPU access. These mechanisms determine starvation risk and interactive response behavior. APPLICATION: SRTF selects the process with the smallest remaining CPU burst. If shorter jobs keep arriving, a long job can be postponed repeatedly, so starvation is possible. Round Robin assigns a time quantum and rotates through the ready queue, giving each waiting process CPU service after bounded turns instead of waiting behind one long FCFS burst. …
qs.rel: SRTF is preemptive and can starve long jobs; non-preemptive SJF is optimal for average waiting among non-preemptive; priority scheduling starves low priority (fix aging). Check each statement.

qs.stem: Which of the following data structures holds the currently allocated instances of resources in Banker’s algorithm of handling deadlocks?
qs.sol:
The Allocation matrix records how many instances of each resource type are currently allocated to each process.

Available records unallocated instances; Max and Need describe demands.
qs.rel: Banker's matrices: Available, Max, Allocation (current holdings), Need = Max - Allocation. Safety algorithm finds a process whose Need <= Work.

qs.stem: Which of the following will be used for a system having multiple instances of a resource type?
qs.sol:
Concept

Deadlock avoidance grants a resource request only if the resulting allocation remains in a safe state.

A safe state has some order in which every process can obtain its remaining maximum need, complete, and release its resources. The suitable method depends on whether each resource type has one instance or several.

Application

Here the intended case has multiple instances of each resource type. The Banker’s algorithm represents Available, Allocation, Max, and Need counts and tentatively tests a request before committing it. The saved value is therefore the Banker’s algorithm. …
qs.rel: Multiple instances of a resource type: use Banker's algorithm. Single instance: resource-allocation graph with claim edges. Both are avoidance methods.

qs.stem: Which of the following occurs between two processes because the outcome of the computation depends on the relative times that the two processes execute their respective critical section?
qs.sol:
A race condition exists when the result depends on the relative timing of concurrent critical-section execution.

Changing that timing can change the result.
qs.rel: Race condition: result depends on relative timing of concurrent processes. Neighbours: critical section, atomic operations, mutex; contrast deadlock and starvation.

qs.stem: Which of the following algorithms is used to solve the critical section problem for n processes?
qs.sol:
Concept

The critical-section problem requires a synchronization mechanism that guarantees three properties for processes sharing a resource: mutual exclusion (at most one process inside the critical section), progress (a waiting process eventually enters), and bounded waiting (no starvation). A general solution must hold for an arbitrary number of processes, n, not just two.

Applying it here

The Bakery algorithm (Lamport, 1974) gives a classic software solution that works for any number of processes n. Each process that wants to enter the critical section draws a numbered token, much like customers taking tickets at a bakery counter. …
qs.rel: Critical section for n processes: Bakery algorithm (Lamport) with ticket numbers. Peterson/Dekker work for 2; hardware TestAndSet works for n. Know the n-process one.

qs.stem:
Match the following.

1

	

Disk scheduling

	

i

	

Shortest Job First
qs.sol:
Shortest Seek Time First belongs to disk scheduling and Shortest Job First to CPU scheduling.

Least Recently Used is a page-replacement method; Banker’s Algorithm is used for deadlock avoidance.
qs.rel: Match algorithm to domain: SSTF/SCAN disk scheduling; SJF/RR CPU scheduling; LRU/FIFO page replacement; Banker's deadlock avoidance; Bakery synchronisation.

qs.stem: Which of the following is true with respect to deadlock avoidance?

opts.A: The avoidance strategy depends on additional information about short-term resource needs.
opts.B: When a process is created in a deadlock, it must declare its minimum claim.
opts.C: With the deadlock avoidance approach, the system is always kept in a safe state.
opts.D: The bakery algorithm is used to deal with deadlock avoidance.

qs.sol:
Deadlock avoidance grants resources only while the system remains in a safe state.

The bakery algorithm addresses mutual exclusion, not deadlock avoidance.
qs.rel: Avoidance keeps system in safe state using prior knowledge of maximum demand. Safe means a safe sequence exists; unsafe may lead to deadlock but not necessarily.

qs.stem:
Match the following.

Column I

	

Column II
qs.sol:
Concept: Operating-system algorithms are classified by the resource or condition they manage.

Scheduling chooses work for a processor or disk; replacement chooses a memory page; deadlock avoidance tests whether resource allocation remains safe.

The algorithm name must therefore be matched to its operation, not just to the word scheduling.

Application: identify the operation named by each algorithm.

SSTF selects the pending disk request requiring the least seek from the current head position; it belongs to disk scheduling.

SJF selects the ready process with the shortest CPU burst; it belongs to CPU scheduling. …
qs.rel: Classify algorithms by resource: Banker's (deadlock avoidance), SCAN (disk), LRU (memory), RR (CPU), Peterson (synchronisation), Dijkstra semaphores.

qs.stem: A computer system has 7 tape drives. There are ‘n’ processes competing for them. Each process may need 2 tape drives. What is the maximum value of ‘n’ for which the system is guaranteed to be deadlock free?
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the printed values are 2, 3, 4 and 1, so none gives the mathematical maximum. The smallest correction replaces 3 with 6. With six processes each may hold one drive, leaving one of seven free; one process can take its second drive, finish and release both. Seven processes could each hold one drive and deadlock.
qs.rel: Guarantee formula: with R resources and n processes each needing at most m, deadlock-free if R >= n(m-1)+1. Here largest n satisfying it. Change m or R and recompute.

qs.stem:
Consider a system with ten units of resource R and three processes: X, Y, and Z. The maximum resource requirement and current allocation to these processes are as follows:
X | Y | Z | Maximum Resource Requirement | 8 | 7 | 5 | Current Allocation | 4 | 1 | 3

Now, consider the following resource requests: 
(i) X makes a request for 2 resource units 
(ii) Y makes a request for 2 resource units 
(iii) Z makes a request for 2 resource units 
For the system to be in safe state, which of the following must be granted?

opts.B: Only requests (i) and (ii) must be granted

qs.sol:
Concept: The Banker's Algorithm keeps a system in a safe state by checking, before granting any request, whether every process's remaining need can eventually be met in some order once processes finish and release resources. Having enough available units for the immediate request is not enough by itself; the requesting process's own leftover need after the grant, and every other process's need, must still be satisfiable in sequence.

Applying it here:

Compute total available units: 10 total minus (4 + 1 + 3) = 8 allocated, giving 2 units available.

Compute the remaining need of each process as Max minus Allocation: X needs 8 − 4 = 4 units, Y needs 7 − 1 = 6 units, Z needs 5 − 3 = 2 units. …
qs.rel: Banker's safety check: compute Available, Need = Max - Allocation, find sequence where each Need <= Work, then Work += Allocation. If none, state unsafe.

qs.sol: Banker's algorithm performs deadlock avoidance. Before granting a resource request, it tests whether the resulting allocation would leave the system in a safe state with some completion sequence; an unsafe request is deferred.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not required condition for a deadlock?
qs.sol: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait. A preemptive system can take a resource away, breaking a necessary condition.

qs.stem: Which set of necessary conditions causes a ‘deadlock’ in an operating system?

opts.A: Blocking send, race condition, hold and wait and RAM overﬂow
opts.B: Blocking send, race condition, cache incoherency and RAM overﬂow
opts.C: Mutual exclusion, no pre-emption, hold and wait, and circular wait
opts.D: Mutual exclusion, race condition, cache incoherency and RAM overﬂow

qs.sol: Deadlock needs mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait simultaneously.

qs.stem: In operating system, Banker’s algorithm is used to
qs.sol:
Concept: Deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance are distinct textbook categories. Prevention structurally removes at least one necessary condition for deadlock, whereas avoidance tests a proposed allocation and permits it only when a safe completion sequence still exists. The Banker's algorithm belongs to the avoidance category.

Application: For each resource request, the algorithm performs a safety test before committing the allocation:

Treat the requested resources as provisionally allocated and update the available and remaining-need values.

Search for an order in which every process can obtain its remaining need, finish, and release its resources. …

qs.stem: A deadlock avoidance algorithm dynamically examines the ______ to ensure that a circular wait condition can never exist.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Deadlock avoidance must predict whether granting a request leaves a safe completion sequence.

It examines the current allocations, available resources and remaining claims before the grant.

qs.stem: The "no preemption" condition in the deadlock problem means that:

opts.A: Resources can be preempted from processes and given to others
opts.B: Once a process holds a resource, it cannot be taken away forcibly
opts.C: Processes can only hold resources for a certain amount of time
opts.D: Processes must release resources after a fixed duration

qs.sol:
No preemption means an allocated resource stays with its holder until the holder voluntarily releases it.

Forced reassignment would break this deadlock condition.

A resource-allocation matrix records how many instances of each resource type are assigned to each process. Deadlock detection compares this allocation with outstanding requests and available resources to determine whether processes can finish.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a solution to the deadlock problem that involves ensuring that processes hold all required resources before starting execution?
qs.sol: Requiring a process to request all resources before it begins prevents hold-and-wait: it cannot hold one resource while waiting for another. Breaking this necessary deadlock condition is a prevention strategy.

qs.stem: According to standard operating-system terminology, which of the following statements is incorrect?

opts.A: Counting semaphore can be used to control access to a finite number of instances of a resource.
opts.B: Reader–writers problem typically arises when several concurrent processes share the database.
opts.D: A computer system is in a safe state only if there exists a safe sequence.

qs.sol:
Note: the printed question does not state which terminology applies to deadlock prevention and deadlock avoidance; we added “According to standard operating-system terminology” so that one option is correct.

Concept: Deadlock prevention removes at least one necessary condition for deadlock through a resource-allocation policy. Deadlock avoidance instead examines each allocation and keeps the system in a safe state.

A safe state has a sequence in which every process can obtain its remaining resources, finish, and release its allocation. Synchronization separately coordinates concurrent access to shared resources. …

qs.stem: If we preempt a resource from a process, the process cannot continue with its normal execution and it must be:
qs.sol: One way deadlock prevention breaks the no-preemption condition is by allowing the operating system to forcibly take a resource away from a process that is holding it, rather than only allowing voluntary release. Because the process's internal execution context, its register values, in-flight computations, and assumptions about the data or resource it was using, was built around continuously holding that resource, simply pausing or removing the process is not enough once the resource is forcibly taken away, the process's progress since it last reached a known-consistent point can no longer be trusted. …

qs.stem: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process i is holding Xi instances of a resource R, 1 ≤ i ≤ n. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all i, process i can place a request for at most Yi additional instances of R while holding the Xi instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that Yp = Yq = 0. Which one of the following conditions guarantees that no other process apart from p and q can complete execution?

opts.A: Xp + Xq < Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
opts.B: Xp + Xq < Max{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}
opts.C: Min(Xp, Xq) ≥ Min{Yk | 1 ≤ k ≤ n, k ≠ p, k ≠ q}

qs.sol: Concept. This item uses the maximum-claim model of deadlock avoidance: every process declares the largest additional amount it may still request, and because the system cannot know in advance that a process will ask for less, a process counts as able to complete only when the free pool can cover that full declared amount. The pool itself grows only when some process finishes and hands back everything it was holding. …

qs.stem: Which one of the following conditions is both necessary and sufficient to conclude that a system is in a safe state?

opts.A: The number of available resources exceeds the maximum resource requirement of every process.
opts.B: No process is currently waiting for a resource.
opts.C: Every process can immediately obtain its maximum resource requirement.
opts.D:
There exists a process order in which every process can obtain its remaining resources and complete execution.

E

Question not attempted

qs.sol: A state is safe exactly when at least one safe sequence exists. Starting with available resources, each process in that sequence can receive its remaining need, finish, and release its allocation for later processes. No process need be immediately able to obtain its maximum total claim simultaneously with all others.

qs.stem: Which of the following is not a valid deadlock prevention scheme ?

opts.A: Release all resources before requesting a new resource.
opts.B: Number the resources uniquely and never request a lower numbered resource than the last one requested.
opts.C: Never request a resource after releasing any resource.
opts.D: Request and all required resources be allocated before execution.

qs.sol: Deadlock prevention breaks at least one necessary deadlock condition. Releasing held resources before a new request removes hold-and-wait; ordered requests remove circular wait; preallocation removes hold-and-wait. A blanket ban on requesting after any release does not prevent a process from holding one resource while requesting another earlier in execution.

To avoid deadlock:

Minimum resources=n×(m−1)+1

Where

n=3(processes)

m=2 (max resources per process)

=3×(2−1)+1

=3+1=4

A resource-allocation graph cycle is not sufficient for deadlock when resource types have multiple instances. A wait-for graph cycle represents circular waiting among processes. The four Coffman conditions together can allow deadlock.

Given

Total tape drives m=6

Each process may need maximum k=3 tape drives

Number of processes = n

To guarantee deadlock freedom, we use the condition:

                     n(k−1)<m

where

n = number of processes

k = maximum resources required by each process

m = total resources

Substitute the values

       n(3−1) < 6

       2n < 6

        n < 3

So the maximum integer value of n is:

               n=2

 Answer: 2

Key idea:  A cycle exists in the graph (for example P1 → R1 → P3 → R2 → P1).
 Identify the cycle: P1 → R1 → P3 → R2 → P1.

topics.deep:
- **Deadlock:** a set of processes each waiting for a resource held by another in the set; none can proceed. **Four necessary (Coffman) conditions - all must hold:** (1) **Mutual exclusion** - at least one resource is non-sharable; (2) **Hold and wait** - holds a resource while requesting others; (3) **No preemption** - resources released only voluntarily; (4) **Circular wait** - cycle P0->P1->...->Pn->P0. Things like "starvation", "aging" or "priority inversion" are **not** deadlock conditions.
- **Resource allocation graph (RAG):** vertices = processes and resource types; request edge P->R, assignment edge R->P. **No cycle = no deadlock.** Cycle with **single instance** per resource = deadlock; cycle with **multiple instances** = possible deadlock only.
- **Handling methods:** (1) **prevention** (negate one condition), (2) **avoidance** (needs advance info; Banker's), (3) **detection and recovery**, (4) **ignore** (ostrich algorithm - Unix/Windows).
- **Prevention - how to break each condition:**
| Condition | Break by | Drawback |
|---|---|---|
| Mutual exclusion | Make resources sharable (read-only files); not possible for printers | Cannot be denied for intrinsically non-sharable |
| Hold and wait | Request all resources at start, or release before requesting new | Low utilisation, starvation |
| No preemption | Preempt held resources if request blocked | Only for state-savable (CPU, memory) |
| Circular wait | Total ordering of resource types, request in increasing order | Inconvenient ordering |
- **Avoidance:** system must stay in **safe state** = exists a **safe sequence** <P1..Pn> where each Pi's remaining need can be satisfied by available + resources held by earlier Pj. **Safe -> no deadlock; unsafe -> may (not must) lead to deadlock.** Single instance per resource: use **RAG with claim edges**; **multiple instances: Banker's algorithm**.
- **Banker's data structures** (n processes, m resource types): **Available[m]**, **Max[n][m]**, **Allocation[n][m]** (currently allocated instances), **Need[n][m] = Max - Allocation**. Safety algorithm: Work=Available; find Pi with Need<=Work not finished; Work += Allocation; repeat.
- **Worked example:** total R = 10; X,Y,Z max 9,5,3 (or similar). If allocation X=3,Y=2,Z=2 -> Available = 10-7 = 3. Needs: X=6, Y=3, Z=1. Z can finish (1<=3): Available=5; Y (3<=5): Available=7; X (6<=7). Safe sequence Z,Y,X.
- **Minimum resources to guarantee no deadlock:** n processes each needing at most m_i units: R >= sum(m_i - 1) + 1. For tape drives: 7 drives, each process needs 2 -> deadlock-free for up to **6** processes (R >= n(2-1)+1 -> n <= 6). With each needing 3: n <= 3. Formula for identical max m: n(m-1)+1 <= R.
- **Detection:** wait-for graph (single instance) cycle detection O(n^2); multiple instances use algorithm like Banker's with Request matrix. **Recovery:** process termination (all or one at a time) or resource preemption (select victim, rollback, starvation concern).
- **Deadlock vs starvation:** deadlock = circular wait, nobody progresses; starvation = indefinite postponement of one process (e.g. low-priority), fixed by **aging**.
- **Belady's anomaly:** under FIFO page replacement, more frames can cause **more page faults** (classic string 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5: 3 frames -> 9 faults, 4 frames -> 10 faults). Pertains to **memory management**, not deadlock. **Stack algorithms (LRU, OPT) are free of it.**
- **Race condition** = outcome depends on timing of concurrent execution (see synchronisation). **Disk scheduling** (SSTF, SCAN) is a *disk* problem; SJF/SRTF are *CPU* scheduling.
- **Critical section requirements** (mutual exclusion, progress, bounded waiting) - "deadlock freedom" is not a listed one. Algorithm for n processes: **Bakery**; for 2: Peterson/Dekker.
- **Preemptive scheduling remarks:** SRTF/preemptive SJF can starve long jobs; it is preemptive; RR is preemptive; FCFS non-preemptive.
- **Typical traps:** unsafe state is not equal to deadlock; cycle in RAG implies deadlock only for single instances; avoidance requires knowledge of maximum demand; prevention is static and conservative.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) find safe sequence from given Allocation/Max/Available; (2) minimum number of resources avoiding deadlock; (3) which condition is broken by ordering resources; (4) RAG cycle with multiple instances; (5) Need matrix calculation; (6) difference between prevention and avoidance; (7) detection algorithm and recovery methods; (8) wait-for graph; (9) ostrich algorithm; (10) deadlock vs starvation.

topics.title: 7. Memory Management & Virtual Memory
topics.theory:
- **Logical (virtual) address** = generated by CPU; **physical address** = in main memory; the **MMU** performs run-time translation (base/relocation register, page table, TLB).
- **Contiguous allocation:** fixed vs variable partitions; **internal fragmentation** = wasted space *inside* an allocated partition; **external fragmentation** = free holes scattered (fixed by **compaction** or paging). Placement: **first-fit, best-fit, worst-fit**.
- **Paging:** fixed-size pages/frames (no external fragmentation, internal only in last page); **segmentation:** variable-size logical units (external fragmentation).
- **Virtual memory:** secondary memory addressed as if part of main memory; **demand paging** loads pages on a page fault; **swapping** moves a whole process: **swap-out** (memory → disk), swap-in (disk → memory).
- **Page replacement:** FIFO, **Optimal (OPT)**, **LRU**, LFU, Clock/second chance, NRU. **Belady's anomaly:** more frames → more page faults; occurs in **FIFO** (not in LRU/OPT — stack algorithms). **Thrashing** = very high page-fault rate, process spends more time paging than executing (fix: working-set model, reduce multiprogramming).
- **Memory manager tasks:** track which parts of memory are used/free, allocate to processes when space available, deallocate.
- **Memory hierarchy speed:** registers > cache (L1 > L2 > L3) > main memory > secondary storage.

qs.stem: Which page replacement algorithm has Belady’s anomaly?
qs.sol: Belady's anomaly occurs when increasing page frames increases page faults. This phenomenon is unique to the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) algorithm. Other algorithms like LRU and Optimal do not exhibit this behavior.
qs.rel: FIFO shows Belady's anomaly (more frames -> more faults, e.g. 1,2,3,4,1,2,5,1,2,3,4,5). Second chance is FIFO-derived. LRU, OPT are stack algorithms without it.

qs.stem: An address generated by the CPU is commonly referred to as a ____.
qs.sol:
The CPU generates logical addresses; the memory-management unit translates them to physical addresses.

This is the address produced by the CPU.
qs.rel: CPU generates logical (virtual) addresses; MMU converts to physical. Binding at compile/load time makes logical = physical; execution-time binding uses relocation register.

qs.stem:
Which of the following are the functions performed by operating system?
 I. Process Management
 II. Memory Management
 III. Security
qs.sol: An operating system performs several key functions to manage computer hardware and software resources. Process Management handles the execution of programs, Memory Management allocates and deallocates memory space to processes, and Security ensures protection against unauthorized access. Therefore, all three listed items (I, II, and III) are functions performed by an operating system.
qs.rel: OS functions include process, memory, file, device management and protection. Applications like word processing or compilers are not OS functions.

qs.stem:
Which of the following page replacement algorithm(s) does not suffer from Belady's anomaly in Operating System?
I. Least-Recently Used (LRU) page replacement.
II. First-In, First-Out (FIFO) page replacement.
qs.sol: LRU page replacement is a stack algorithm and does not suffer from Belady's anomaly. FIFO can suffer from Belady's anomaly, so only statement I is correct.
qs.rel: LRU and OPT are stack algorithms: no Belady anomaly. FIFO has it. LRU needs hardware support (counter/stack); OPT cannot be implemented in practice.

qs.stem: When there is a memory wastage within the memory partition itself then it known as ______.
qs.sol:
Concept

Fragmentation describes memory that cannot be used efficiently because of how allocation divides or sizes memory. Internal waste is tied to the size of an allocated block, whereas external waste is tied to the arrangement of free blocks.

Application

Suppose the allocator provides a fixed 100 KB partition to a process that requests 80 KB.

The process uses 80 KB, while 20 KB remains reserved inside the same allocated partition.

That 20 KB cannot be assigned independently to another process while the partition remains allocated.

Waste inside the allocated block is therefore classified as internal fragmentation. …
qs.rel: Internal fragmentation: waste inside an allocated block (fixed partitions, last page). External: free holes not contiguous (variable partitions, segmentation). Compaction fixes external.

qs.stem: The rate at which page fault occurs is known as __________.
qs.sol: In demand-paging systems, a page fault occurs whenever a running process references a page that is not currently resident in main memory, forcing the OS to fetch it from secondary storage. As long as a process has enough frames for its working set, faults stay infrequent. When a process (or the whole system) is starved of frames, the OS ends up servicing faults back-to-back, and the specific named state in which the CPU spends more time handling these faults than executing processes — collapsing throughput even while the system looks 'busy' — has its own distinct term in OS terminology, separate from the general mechanisms of paging, swapping, or compaction. …
qs.rel: Page-fault rate p affects EAT = (1-p)*ma + p*fault service time. High rate leads to thrashing. Related: working set, page-fault frequency, demand paging.

qs.stem:
Which of the following is a primary task of memory management system?
 I. It keeps track of which parts of the memory are currently being used
 II. When space is available, it allocates memory to the programs that are next to be loaded
qs.sol: Memory management system performs key tasks to ensure efficient use of memory. It keeps track of which parts of memory are currently in use (Statement I) to prevent conflicts and ensure data integrity. When memory space becomes available, it allocates memory to programs that are ready to be loaded (Statement II), enabling smooth execution of processes. Both tasks are essential for effective memory handling in an operating system.
qs.rel: Memory manager tracks used/free memory, decides allocation, allocates and deallocates, protects. Also swapping and virtual memory. Not its job: CPU scheduling.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a storage allocation scheme in which secondary memory can be addressed as though it were part of the main memory?
qs.sol:
The correct answer is Option 1: Virtual Memory.

Virtual Memory is a memory management technique that creates an illusion for users and applications that the computer has a very large, contiguous main memory. It allows the system to address secondary memory (like an HDD or SSD) as if it were part of the main memory (RAM).

This is achieved by mapping "virtual addresses" used by a program into "physical addresses" in computer memory. When the RAM is full, the operating system moves inactive data to a space on the secondary storage (often called a page file or swap partition), bringing it back only when needed.
qs.rel: Virtual memory lets secondary memory be addressed like main memory; implemented by demand paging or segmentation. Neighbours: page table, TLB, swapping, thrashing.

qs.stem: ______ is a process of lifting the process from memory and placing it on disk.
qs.sol:
Concept

Swapping is a memory-management technique in which the operating system moves an entire process between main memory (RAM) and a backing store on disk. Moving a process out of RAM onto disk is called swapping out (swap-out); bringing it back from disk into RAM is called swapping in (swap-in).

Application

The stem describes lifting a whole process from memory and placing it on disk. Matching this to the definition above, transferring a complete process from RAM to disk is precisely the swap-out operation, so the answer is Swapping out. It temporarily frees physical RAM for other processes while the swapped-out process waits on disk. …
qs.rel: Swapping moves a process between memory and backing store (roll out/roll in). Medium-term scheduler decides; swap time is dominated by transfer time.

qs.stem: Which of the following hardware is used for run-time mapping from virtual to physical addresses?
qs.sol: Run-time mapping from virtual or logical addresses to physical addresses is done by the memory management unit (MMU). The MMU uses mechanisms such as page tables and TLB support to translate addresses during execution. Therefore, option B is correct.
qs.rel: MMU maps logical to physical addresses at run time (relocation register, page table). TLB caches page-table entries. Compiler/assembler/linker work at earlier stages.

qs.stem: Which of the following is a part of the classic process that keeps track of code execution within the framework?
qs.sol:
A thread is an execution path within a process and tracks the running code.

A process can contain multiple threads.
qs.rel: Thread tracks execution path within a process (PC, registers, stack). Process holds resources; thread is unit of CPU. Same facts as thread questions in process topic.

qs.stem: If a memory partition of size 80k is allocated to a process of size 60k then the 20k of the partition is wasted and cannot be allocated to any process. It is called __________.
qs.sol:
When a process is allocated more memory than it needs, the unused portion within that specific block remains wasted.

This unused space inside an allocated partition is known as internal fragmentation, distinct from external fragmentation which involves scattered free blocks.
qs.rel: Unused part of allocated partition = internal fragmentation (80K-60K=20K). Fixed partitioning causes it; variable partitioning causes external fragmentation instead.

qs.stem: The memory resident components of an operating system are commonly known as the ______ of the operating system.
qs.sol: The Kernel is the central, core component of an operating system. It is the first part of the OS to load into memory during booting and remains memory-resident (staying in RAM the entire time the computer is running). Its primary role is to manage the communication between software (applications) and hardware (CPU, memory, devices).
qs.rel: Memory-resident OS core = kernel. Other parts (utilities, system programs) are loaded when needed. Kernel includes memory, process, device management and is always in RAM.

qs.stem: The process in an operating system in which the output of any program is not printed directly on the printer but dumped onto a reserved area of a disk is known as ______.
qs.sol: Spooling stands for Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line. It is the process where output from programs is buffered onto a reserved area of disk before being sent to devices like printers, rather than printed directly.
qs.rel: Spooling = Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line: output saved to disk and printed later. Buffering uses memory. Spooling lets CPU overlap with slow I/O devices.

qs.stem: The process of organising the contents of each file into contiguous regions and creating larger areas of free space on the hard disk is called ______ and ______ is the process of making computer files take up less space on your computer by reducing the size of the file.
qs.sol: The first part of the question describes Defragmentation, which organizes file contents into contiguous regions to create larger areas of free space. The second part describes Compression, which reduces the size of computer files to save storage space.
qs.rel: Defragmentation arranges file blocks contiguously and merges free space, improving access. Compaction is its memory counterpart for external fragmentation.

qs.stem: If two non-continuous free partition of size ‘a’ and ‘b’ are available. A process of size ‘c’ cannot be allocated even when a + b > c, a < c and b < c. This problem is known as __________.
qs.sol:
When total free memory exceeds process size but blocks are non-contiguous, allocation fails. This occurs because no single partition is large enough to hold the process.

This specific problem is defined as external fragmentation in operating systems.
qs.rel: External fragmentation: total free space >= request but not contiguous. Remedies: compaction, paging, segmentation. 50-percent rule: about one third lost with first fit.

qs.stem: Which of the following dynamic allocation methods suffers from external fragmentation?
qs.sol: First fit and best fit can leave separated free holes, so the paper keys their pair. Worst fit can also cause external fragmentation; consequently the printed pair “Worst fit and best fit” is technically defensible and the item is ambiguous.
qs.rel: Dynamic partition methods first/best/worst fit all suffer external fragmentation. Paging avoids it. Worst fit leaves large leftover holes; best fit leaves tiny holes.

qs.stem:
Match the following:

List-1

	

List-2
qs.sol:
Correct answer: I-B, II-A, III-C

Long-term scheduler -> Job scheduling: It admits jobs/processes into the system for execution.

Medium-term scheduler -> Swapping: It suspends and resumes processes by swapping them out of and into memory.

Short-term scheduler -> CPU scheduling: It selects the next ready process to run on the CPU.

Therefore, the correct matching is I-B, II-A, III-C.
qs.rel: Schedulers: long-term = job scheduling, short-term = CPU scheduling, medium-term = swapping. Matching adds degree of multiprogramming and frequency.

qs.stem:
A free list contains three memory areas of sizes 6 KB, 15 KB and 12 KB.
 The next three memory requests are for 10 KB, 2 KB and 14 KB.
 Which of the memory allocation strategy would be able to accommodate all the three requests?
qs.sol:
Request 10 KB: Allocated to the smallest block that fits (12 KB). Remaining: [6 KB, 15 KB, 2 KB].

Request 2 KB: Allocated to the smallest block that fits (2 KB). Remaining: [6 KB, 15 KB, 0 KB].

Request 14 KB: Allocated to the smallest block that fits (15 KB). Remaining: [6 KB, 1 KB, 0 KB].

Result: All requests accommodated.
qs.rel: Placement strategies: first fit (first adequate hole), best fit (smallest adequate), worst fit (largest). Request goes to a different hole each time; recompute leftover each step.

qs.stem: If there are 64 segments, each of size 2KB, then how many bits should a logical address have?
qs.sol: In a segmented memory system, the logical address consists of segment number bits and offset bits. With 64 segments, log2(64) equals 6 bits for the segment number. Each segment is 2KB (2048 bytes), requiring log2(2048) equals 11 bits for the offset. Adding these together gives a total logical address size of 6 plus 11, which equals 17 bits.
qs.rel: Segmented address bits = bits for segment number + offset bits: log2(64)=6 and log2(2KB)=11 gives 17. Variant: page number bits plus offset bits in paging.

qs.stem:
Identify the true statement(s):

(i) Fixed partition memory strategy suffers from external fragmentation.

(ii) Variable partition memory strategy suffers from internal fragmentation.

(iii) In variable partition memory strategy, when the system is initialised, the primary memory is configured as a single large block.
qs.sol:
Fixed partitions chiefly create internal fragmentation; variable partitions chiefly create external fragmentation.

Initially, variable-partition memory is one large free block, so only the third statement holds.
qs.rel: Fixed partitions cause internal fragmentation; variable partitions cause external. Paging has small internal only; segmentation has external only. Check statements against this.

qs.stem: The user process is 100 MB in size and the backing store is a standard hard disk with a transfer rate of 50 MB per second. The swap time is 200 milliseconds. What is the total swap time (ignoring other disk performance aspects)?
qs.sol:
CONCEPT: A swap moves a process once from memory to the backing store and once from the backing store back to memory. Transfer time equals data size divided by transfer rate.

APPLICATION: One 100 MB transfer takes 100 MB ÷ 50 MB/s = 2 s = 2000 ms.

APPLICATION: Swapping out and then swapping in requires 2 s + 2 s = 4 s = 4000 ms.

CROSS-CHECK: The textbook example with these same values reports about 4,000 milliseconds when both directions are included; the 200-millisecond figure is stated separately and does not replace the transfer calculation.

Result: 4000 milliseconds.
qs.rel: Swap time = size / transfer rate (+ latency); swap out + swap in doubles it. Larger process or slower disk increases it; context switch time is dominated by swapping.

qs.stem: Which of the following statements is INCORRECT about memory protection?

opts.A: It is used to protect the operating system from users' processes.
opts.B: This protection can be provided by using a relocation register along with a limit register.
opts.C: The relocation register contains the largest physical address.
opts.D: The limit register contains the range of the logical addresses.

qs.sol:
Concept

A base-and-limit (relocation + limit) scheme protects memory by bounding every process to a contiguous region. The relocation (base) register holds the SMALLEST physical address allocated to the process, and the limit register holds the RANGE (size) of the valid logical addresses. The MMU forms a physical address as base + logical address, and admits the access only while the logical address is strictly less than the limit; otherwise it traps.

Applying it to each statement

"Used to protect the OS from user processes" — true: bounding each process to its own region is exactly what memory protection does. …
qs.rel: Memory protection uses base+limit registers loaded only in kernel mode by privileged instructions; every user address checked by hardware; user cannot modify them.

qs.stem: Which of the following statement is correct for a ‘Volume Control block’ in File-System Implementation?

opts.A: It is used to organize the files
opts.B: It has a unique identifier number to allow association with a directory entry
opts.C: It contains the number of block in the partition
opts.D: It can contain information needed by the system to boot an operating system from that volume

qs.sol: A volume control block stores volume/partition metadata, including information such as the number of blocks in the partition.
qs.rel: Volume control block (superblock) holds volume info: block count, block size, free-block count and pointers. Contrast directory structure and per-file FCB/inode.

qs.stem:
Consider the following page reference string: 
1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 4, 1 
Assume that there are three page frames which are initially empty. Let LRU, FIFO and OPTIMAL denote the number of page faults under the corresponding page replacement strategy. Then, which of the following expressions is true?
qs.sol: With three initially empty frames and reference string 1, 2, 3, 2, 4, 1, 3, 2, 4, 1: FIFO gives 6 page faults, LRU gives 9 page faults, and OPTIMAL gives 5 page faults. Hence the true relation is OPTIMAL < FIFO < LRU.
qs.rel: Page-fault counting: simulate frames step by step, mark F/H. FIFO replaces oldest; LRU least recently used; OPT farthest next use. Compare results across algorithms.

qs.stem: A 500 kbyte memory is managed using variable memory partitions and compaction is allowed. It is currently using 2 partitions of sizes 100 kbytes and 130 kbytes respectively. The smallest allocation request in kbytes that could be denied is _____.
qs.sol: First, calculate the total used memory by adding the partition sizes: 100 KB + 130 KB = 230 KB. Next, determine the available free space by subtracting used memory from total memory: 500 KB - 230 KB = 270 KB. Since compaction is allowed, the free space can be consolidated into a single contiguous block of 270 KB. Therefore, any allocation request up to 270 KB can be satisfied. The smallest request that cannot be accommodated is one byte larger than the available space, which is 271 KB.
qs.rel: Variable partitions with compaction: sum used partitions, free = total - used; after compaction free space is contiguous, so a request fits if total free >= request.

7, 0, 1, 0, 2, 7, 1, 0, 1, 2

qs.stem: With respect to accessing speed, which of the following represents the correct relationships between different categories of cache memory?
qs.sol: Cache memory access speed decreases as the level increases from L1 to L3. L1 cache is closest to the CPU and offers the fastest access, while L3 is furthest away with slower speeds.
qs.rel: Memory hierarchy speed: registers > L1 > L2 > L3 > RAM > SSD/HDD; cost per byte and speed fall, size rises downward. L1 is fastest and smallest.

qs.stem:
A computer system has 1000 KB of contiguous main memory, initially empty. Jobs are allocated in arrival order and are not relocated or compacted. The sequence is:

Job 1 arrives and requires 200 KB.

Job 2 arrives and requires 350 KB.

Job 3 arrives and requires 300 KB.

Job 1 finishes.

Job 4 arrives and requires 120 KB.

Job 5 arrives and requires 150 KB.

Job 6 arrives and requires 70 KB.

Between first-fit and best-fit, which policy can allocate all arriving jobs in this sequence?
qs.sol:
Concept

In contiguous allocation, first-fit selects the first hole in address order that is large enough, whereas best-fit selects the smallest hole that is large enough.

External fragmentation is compared by tracing the ordered hole sizes after each allocation; total free memory alone is not sufficient when no single hole is large enough.

Source note: this stored edition modifies the official-paper comparison to ask whether all arrivals can be allocated without relocation or compaction.

Application

The initially empty memory is one 1000 KB hole. The first three allocations leave 1000 − 200 − 350 − 300 = 150 KB at the high-address end. …
qs.rel: Contiguous allocation simulation: first fit takes first adequate hole, best fit smallest, worst fit largest; track holes after each job and note which request fails.

qs.stem: Which of the following is an example of volatile memory in a computer system?
qs.sol: Volatile memory loses its contents when power is removed. RAM holds working data only while powered.

qs.stem: The main/primary memory of a computer is also called :
qs.sol: Main memory is RAM, the directly addressable working memory used by active programs. A hard disk and pen drive are secondary storage; cache is a smaller, faster layer.

qs.stem: Belady's anomaly can occur in which page replacement algorithm ?

opts.D:
FIFO (First-In, First-Out)

E

Question not attempted

qs.sol:
Belady's anomaly means more frames can sometimes cause more faults.

FIFO lacks the stack/inclusion property, so its replacement order can produce that counterintuitive behavior.

qs.stem: The mechanism that brings a page into memory only when it is needed is ______.
qs.sol:
Concept: Virtual memory permits a process to use pages that are not all resident in physical memory. A page table marks whether each page is present, and a reference to an absent page raises a page fault.

The operating system can respond to that fault by fetching the referenced page from backing storage. This policy of loading a page when it is demanded is called demand paging.

The process references a virtual page; the page-table entry shows that it is absent from physical memory.

The resulting page fault transfers control to the operating system, which locates the page on backing storage. …

Modified from the official paper: the printed stem says a process moves from main memory to secondary memory, which describes swapping and has no listed response. Changing “process” to “page” and reversing the transfer direction makes the credited response correct. Demand paging loads a page from secondary memory into main memory only when it is needed. General paging does not require an on-demand transfer; threads and segmentation describe different concepts.

On demand, a page is loaded from secondary memory into main memory; select “Demand paging”.
Virtual memory uses a portion of the hard disk as an extension of the computer’s main memory. Therefore, the mechanism described is virtual memory.

qs.stem: Which of the following page replacement algorithms requires futuristic information about page references?
qs.sol:
Solution:  The Optimal page replacement algorithm replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time in the future.
 Hence, it requires knowledge of future page references, which is not available in real systems. For this reason, the Optimal algorithm is theoretical and used as a benchmark; practical algorithms such as Least Recently Used (LRU) try to approximate its behavior using past access information.

qs.stem: The page replacement policy that sometimes leads to more page faults when the size of memory is increased is:
qs.sol: The correct answer is FIFO. This policy exhibits Belady's Anomaly, where increasing memory frames can paradoxically increase page faults under certain reference strings. Other policies like LRU avoid this behavior.

qs.stem: When a process is moved from main memory to the secondary storage, it is called:
qs.sol: Moving a process image between main memory and secondary storage is swapping.

qs.stem: What causes thrashing to occur?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Insufficient frames cause repeated faults for a process’s working set.

The system spends much of its time moving pages rather than doing useful work.

That excessive paging is thrashing.

qs.stem: An overlay is

opts.B: A single contiguous memory that was used in old days for running large programs by swapping
opts.D: Overloading the system with many files

qs.sol: The printed memory/swapping description is an imprecise description of an overlay. More precisely, mutually exclusive program parts share one memory region and are loaded when needed; here, "swapping" is read as replacing those program parts in that region. This lets a program larger than that region execute. The provisional key pointed to this intended idea; no final key was found.

qs.stem: An overlay is
qs.sol:
Blocked state: the process is waiting for an event such as I/O completion.

After I/O completion: the event has occurred, so the process becomes eligible to run again. However, it must wait for CPU scheduling.

Therefore, the process moves from the blocked state to the ready state.

Belady’s anomaly is the counterintuitive behavior in which adding more page frames can increase the number of page faults, especially with FIFO page replacement. Therefore, it points out that the page fault may increase as the number of allocated frames increases.

Modified from the official paper: A process larger than a fixed partition would not fit; the stem now asks about the unused space left inside a partition by a smaller process. That unused allocated space is internal fragmentation.

qs.stem: In multiprogramming with fixed partitions, if a process requires less memory than is available in its assigned partition, it may lead to:
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: The printed more-than premise cannot describe internal fragmentation; less-than is the minimal correction. A process smaller than its fixed partition leaves unused space inside that partition: “Fragmentation.” “Deadlock” is a resource-wait cycle, not unused allocated memory.

The phenomenon where increasing the number of frames leads to an increase in page faults is known as Belady's anomaly. This anomaly occurs only in certain page replacement algorithms.

FIFO (First In First Out) is the only algorithm among the given options that exhibits Belady's anomaly. In FIFO, the oldest page is replaced, and under certain access patterns, adding more frames can result in more page faults due to the replacement policy.

LRU (Least Recently Used) and OPT (Optimal) do not exhibit this anomaly because they are based on usage patterns that avoid such counterintuitive behavior. MRU (Most Recently Used) also does not show Belady's anomaly. …

qs.stem: In _________ page replacement algorithm, the page that will not be used for the longest period of time is replaced whenever a page fault occurs.
qs.sol:
Concept — every page-replacement policy is defined by a single eviction key: at a page fault the policy computes one value for each page currently resident in a frame and discards the page whose value is extreme. The classical policies differ only in what that value is measured from — the access history already recorded, the order in which pages arrived, an access count, or the sequence of references still to come.

Applying it here — the blank must be filled by the policy whose eviction key is "how far ahead this page is next referenced". …

qs.stem: Dirty bit is used to show the

opts.D: page that is modified after being loaded into cache memory

qs.sol:
Answer: page that is modified after being loaded into cache memory

Explanation: The dirty bit is a flag associated with a page/frame that shows whether the page has been changed (written to) in memory since it was loaded or last saved to disk. It helps the operating system decide if the page needs to be written back to disk before being evicted.

When the dirty bit is set: A write to the page has occurred, so the in-memory copy is newer than the on-disk copy.

On eviction: If the dirty bit is set, the OS must write the page back to disk (write-back). If it is clear, the page can be discarded without writing. …

qs.stem: Which memory management technique uses fixed-sized blocks of memory, allowing processes to be loaded into any available block?
qs.sol: Paging is the memory-management technique that uses fixed-size blocks. Logical memory is divided into pages, and physical memory is divided into frames of the same size. A process can be loaded into any available frames, so contiguous physical memory is not required.

qs.stem: In virtual memory paging, page size and frame size have which of the following relations?

opts.C: The page size is exactly half of the frame size
opts.D: The page size is twice the frame size

qs.sol:
Answer:  Page size must be equal to frame size.
 Key points:
 Memory is divided into pages (logical memory) and frames (physical memory).

qs.stem: Segmentation is a memory management technique in which memory is divided into:
qs.sol:
Concept: A disk scheduler chooses which pending request the disk head services next. First-come, first-served (FCFS) keeps a first-in, first-out queue: arrival time determines service order, regardless of track distance. Seek time grows with the head movement needed between successive tracks, so arrival order alone does not optimize total movement or every request’s wait.

Application: Suppose the head starts at track 50 and requests for tracks 100 and 51 are both pending when the scheduler chooses, with track 100 having arrived first. FCFS services track 100 first, then track 51; the head travels 50 tracks and then 49 tracks, for 99 tracks of movement. …

qs.stem: Segmentation is a memory management technique in which memory is divided into:
qs.sol: Segmentation divides a program or memory space into logical segments such as code, data, and stack. These segments are variable in size, unlike paging where memory is divided into fixed-size pages and frames. Hence, segmentation divides memory into variable-sized blocks of memory.
A page table maps each virtual page number to a physical frame number. The processor combines that frame with the page offset to form the physical address.

qs.stem: What is compaction?

opts.A: A technique for overcoming internal fragmentation
opts.C: A technique for overcoming external fragmentation
opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Compaction relocates allocated memory blocks together, collecting scattered free holes into one region.

This addresses external fragmentation.

qs.stem: The technique of operating system to temporary remove inactive programs from memory of computer system:
qs.sol: Swapping is the operating system technique used to temporarily remove inactive programs from main memory by moving them to secondary storage. This process frees up RAM space for active processes, unlike scheduling which manages CPU time allocation.

qs.stem: When a program is allocated a memory hole that is bigger than needed, then it is called:
qs.sol: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated memory is larger than required, leaving unused space inside the allocated block.

qs.stem: What is a page in paging?

opts.A: A fixed-size block of virtual memory
opts.B: A fixed-size block of physical memory
opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages.

Physical memory is divided into frames of the same size.

The question asks for the virtual block.

qs.stem: Which storage allocation strategy allocates the largest available block of memory to a process, ensuring that the remaining space is maximized?
qs.sol:
Worst fit selects the largest free block for each allocation.

The remainder of that block is consequently as large as possible among available choices.

qs.stem: _______ method is used to map logical addresses of variable length onto physical memory.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Variable-length logical regions correspond to program segments such as code and data.

A segment number and offset map through a segment table to physical memory.

qs.stem: Which of the following is NOT a memory management technique used by operating systems?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Paging and segmentation are schemes used to map and allocate memory.

Fragmentation is wasted space that can arise from allocation, not itself an allocation scheme.

The question asks for the item outside the management-technique category.

qs.stem: In operating-system memory management, an overlay is:
qs.sol: Modified from the official paper: the offered claim that hardware cannot execute programs directly was false; it has been replaced with the command interpreter's actual role. A command interpreter reads a user's textual command, parses it, and asks the operating system to perform the requested action. The processor executes machine instructions, while the command interpreter provides the user-facing command interface.

qs.stem: In operating-system memory management, an overlay is:

opts.A: A technique in which mutually exclusive program modules share the same memory region and are loaded as needed
opts.B: A condition caused by storing too many files in the system
opts.C: One fixed physical memory address reserved for a program
opts.D: A permanent component of the operating-system kernel

qs.sol:
Concept

An overlay is a memory-management technique used when a program is larger than the available main memory. The program is divided into modules that are not required simultaneously; those mutually exclusive modules reuse the same memory region and are loaded when needed.

Application

The description of mutually exclusive program modules sharing one region states this mechanism: only the required module occupies the reusable region at a given time.

Contrast

Storing many files concerns file-system or secondary-storage capacity, not the loading of program modules into main memory. …

qs.stem: _____ is used to shift processes so they are contiguous, and all free memory is in one block.

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Compaction is a technique used in memory management to rearrange processes in memory so that all free memory is consolidated into a single contiguous block. This helps in reducing external fragmentation and allows for efficient allocation of memory to new processes.

Contiguous memory allocation refers to a memory management technique in which, whenever a user process requests memory, a single contiguous block of memory is allocated to that process according to its requirement.

qs.stem: Copying a process from memory to disk to allow space for other processes is called ______.
qs.sol: In a time sharing operating system, processes are allocated CPU time in fixed time slices. When a process's time slice expires, it is preempted by the scheduler. The process does not terminate, block, or suspend; instead, it is moved back to the ready queue to wait for the next CPU allocation. This ensures fair CPU sharing among all processes. …

qs.stem: Copying a process from memory to disk to allow space for other processes is called ______.
qs.sol:
Moving an entire process from main memory to disk temporarily to free memory space is called swapping.

Demand paging and page fault are related to virtual memory, not whole-process movement.

Deadlock is a condition of resource waiting, not memory transfer.

qs.stem: Which storage allocation strategy allows multiple processes to reside in memory simultaneously without requiring contiguous memory blocks?
qs.sol: Paging divides virtual memory into pages and physical memory into frames. A process’s pages may occupy nonadjacent frames, so several processes can reside in memory without contiguous blocks.

qs.stem: In process swapping in operating system, what is the residing location of swap space ?
qs.sol: Swap space resides on secondary storage, ordinarily a disk, so memory pages or processes can be moved out of RAM.

qs.stem: How is the TLB typically organized?

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Concept: A translation lookaside buffer (TLB) caches virtual-page to physical-frame translations so that a processor can reuse a translation without walking the page table.

Cache associativity specifies where an entry may be placed and which tags must be compared during lookup. It is separate from what information the cache stores.

Application: In the conventional fully associative TLB model, a translation may occupy any available entry.

For an example lookup, suppose virtual page 7 is cached as physical frame 23. The virtual address is split into a virtual-page number and a page offset.

The requested virtual-page tag is compared with the valid stored tags in parallel. …

qs.stem: What is a segment base in segmentation?

opts.A: The starting address of a segment in physical memory
opts.B: The starting address of a segment in virtual memory

qs.stem: The main advantage of the overlay technique in memory management is that it allows:

opts.A: Processes to be loaded into memory as a whole
opts.C: Large programs to be executed on systems with limited memory
opts.D: Processes to communicate directly with each other

qs.sol:
Concept

Overlaying is a memory-management technique in which a program is split into self-contained modules called overlays, only some of which must reside in main memory at any instant. Mutually exclusive parts of the program share the same physical memory region, taking turns: an overlay is loaded over (replacing) a previous one when its routines are needed.

Application

The total program text may be far larger than the available physical memory, yet only the overlay (or overlays) currently executing plus the resident root must fit. …

qs.stem: Memory in which any location can be reached in a fixed amount of time after specifying its address is called

opts.D:
More than one of the above

E

None of the above

qs.sol:
Sequential storage must traverse earlier locations, so its access time varies.

Random-access memory can reach a specified address directly in essentially fixed time.

Both the first-fit and best-fit strategies for memory allocation suffer from external fragmentation. As processes are loaded into and removed from memory, the free memory space gets broken into small, non-contiguous pieces.

Concept: Best fit places a request in the smallest free hole that can contain it. A split leaves the unused portion as a separate free hole.

External fragmentation occurs when free memory is divided into pieces that are individually too small for a request, even when their combined size is sufficient.

Suppose the free holes are 10 KB and 18 KB, and a process needs 9 KB. Both can hold the process, so best fit selects the smaller 10 KB hole.

Splitting that hole gives 9 KB to the process and leaves a 1 KB free hole. Repeated choices of this kind can accumulate small remainders that cannot serve larger requests. …

qs.stem: What is coalescing?

opts.A: It is a second strategy for allocating kernel memory.
opts.B: The buddy system allocates memory from a fixed size segment consisting of physically contiguous pages.
opts.C: Kernel memory is often allocated from a free-memory pool different from the list used to satisfy ordinary user mode processes.
opts.D: An advantage of the buddy system is how quickly adjacent buddies can be combined to form larger segments using this technique.

qs.sol:
In dynamic memory allocation, free memory can become fragmented into many small blocks that individually cannot satisfy a larger request, even though enough total free memory exists. Coalescing is the general technique of merging two or more adjacent free blocks into a single larger free block, so that fragmented free space can be reused for bigger requests without relocating or compacting other memory.

The buddy system splits memory into blocks whose sizes are powers of two. Whenever a block is freed, the allocator checks whether its buddy — the adjacent block created when the same parent block was originally split — is also free. …

The data structure used to represent the allocation status of main memory is a memory map. A memory map keeps track of which portions of memory are free and which are allocated. It is essential for memory management in operating systems.

opts.D:
